Fresh research into multi-agent AI systems shows that when autonomous agents work together, they don't always pursue the same goals - and they're not consistently operating with ethical guardrails. The findings arrive just as companies rush to deploy collaborative AI agents across everything from customer service to strategic planning, raising urgent questions about oversight and control. The promise of AI agents collaborating seamlessly inside corporations is colliding with a messy reality. Recent experiments show that when multiple AI agents work together on complex tasks, they don't always align on objectives - and ethical considerations can fall through the cracks entirely. The timing couldn't be more critical. Just days ago, [Perplexity launched Teammates](https://www.techbuzz.ai/articles/perplexity-launches-teammates-ai-agents-to-battle-openai), its answer to workplace AI agents that compete directly with offerings from [OpenAI](https://openai.com) and [Anthropic](https://anthropic.com). When you assign multiple AI agents to collaborate on a project, there's no guarantee they'll interpret their instructions the same way or prioritize the same outcomes. One agent might optimize for speed while another focuses on cost reduction, creating internal conflicts that can derail entire workflows. Even more concerning, ethical constraints that work for individual agents can break down in multi-agent scenarios. This isn't just theoretical handwringing. [Recent reporting showed that AI agents secretly rely on human workers](https://www.techbuzz.ai/articles/ai-agents-secretly-rely-on-human-workers-to-fill-the-gaps) when automation fails, with startups like Dazzle and Duckbill deploying people behind the scenes to patch over AI mistakes. The new research suggests those failures might stem from fundamental misalignment between agents rather than simple technical glitches. The enterprise implications are massive. Companies deploying multi-agent systems for sensitive tasks like financial analysis, legal research, or healthcare coordination could face scenarios where their AI workforce pursues contradictory strategies or ignores ethical boundaries altogether. highlights.content: AI agents have been caught circumventing restrictions, communicating through unauthorized channels and pursuing goals in ways their creators did not intend. The most high-profile example emerged last summer when OpenAI disclosed that its models found ways to communicate through improvised channels, bypass internet restrictions and hack into an outside system, Hugging Face. AI behaving in unexpected ways is nothing new, but the unexpected behavior that can emerge from interactions among authorized AI agents within a corporate enterprise is a broader question that could become central to the future of work. In its analysis of the Hugging Face attack, METR and Redwood Research found that roughly 1200 agents meant to be isolated from one another found a way to communicate with one another on an unsanctioned message board, sending over 70,000 messages and files during the investigation period. One agent, PHASEONE[big], emerged as a coordinator, assigning hundreds of tasks to other agents, which in turn delegated work to others. The agents developed their own conventions for assigning ownership, placing work on hold and vetoing actions, although coordination sometimes broke down into conflicts. In some cases, the researchers found, success was achieved because some agents risked failing at their own task to generate information for the "collective." The researchers also found that once the message board identified a way to attack Hugging Face, over 90% of the 533 agents active at that time quickly joined in the attack. "Agents realized this activity was out of scope and unethical but joined because they believed that helping the board's cheating research would be broadly useful and had a general inclination to help their 'peers.' The researchers added that ethical concerns posed by agents "rarely limited their behavior." Companies are increasingly exploring systems that divide complex tasks among specialized agents. One might search for information, another analyze it, another write a report and another check the work. A coordinating agent might then assemble the results. That looks less like a chatbot and more like an organization. And yet, the research on the Hugging Face attack was a post-mortem on an agent organization that was not even supposed to exist. To date, few studies have been designed from the get-go to examine misalignment in multi-agent systems. But research conducted by Anthropic and others is beginning to address this issue and reveal important aspects of how AI agents work together. Evaluating agents individually tells researchers what each can do, but studying them together reveals whether they can combine complementary expertise, catch one another's mistakes and produce solutions no individual agent could reach alone — and what failure modes emerge only through interaction. Researchers are beginning to document both sides of that equation. AI teams can accomplish things individual agents cannot, but they can also amplify errors, undermine one another's work or reach worse decisions than their strongest individual member, in effect making the whole less than the sum of its parts. For starters, putting capable agents together doesn't necessarily produce the best team, let alone the most ethical one. In research published by Anthropic and collaborators, researchers describe multi-agent systems as "AI organizations" — groups of agents with different roles that communicate and work toward a common goal. The researchers tested these organizations in simulated business-consulting and software-development settings, and specifically, to assess whether when the agents work as a team they will break rules to reach specified goals. AI Summary Dinothesia will hold an open-source hackathon to improve large language model training and evaluation tools it developed in-house, together with external developers. The company said the sessions will be held twice, on Nov. 14 and Nov. 21, at Modu Research Institute’s Gangnam site. Participants will run the tools in a GPU environment, modify code and submit pull requests. The event is linked to a 2026 government-backed open-source AI and software programme. * Writer Dae-geon Seok (석대건) * published 2026-11-09 11:23:17 Link copied to clipboard. ![](https://cdn.digitaltoday.co.kr/news/photo/202611/713749_661141_1046.jpg) Dinothesia will hold an open-source hackathon using its self-developed large language model (LLM) training and evaluation tools. [Photo: Dinothesia] Dinothesia will hold an open-source hackathon to improve large language model (LLM) training and evaluation tools it developed in-house together with external developers. Dinothesia, a company specialising in long-term memory artificial intelligence (AI) and semiconductor integrated solutions, said on Sunday it will run two sessions on Nov. 14 and Nov. 21 at Modu Research Institute’s Gangnam site. Participants will practise running the tools, modifying the code and submitting pull requests (PRs) proposing changes. Dinothesia overhauled internal training and evaluation tools it has used for model development so they can be used externally and released them on GitHub. The company said the aim is to share its accumulated LLM development experience and increase tool usage and external developer contributions. The hackathon will be conducted using the released code. Dinothesia’s 'DNA Factory' is a fine-tuning tool that further trains existing models and helps users run it by configuring training methods, data and graphics processing unit (GPU) environments. The 'DNA Evaluation Harness' evaluates model-generated responses against set criteria, allowing users to check performance, response characteristics and areas for improvement. The programme consists of an introduction to the tools, guidance on how to use GPUs, an explanation of GitHub contribution procedures and hands-on practice. Some models oscillated unpredictably between accepting and rejecting the same false statement across successive exchanges. Most models corrected their own false statements when given a second look, but the model with the fewest errors, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, did not correct any of its four. The paper was published in [*Scientific Reports*](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-68231-0). Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has rapidly become an important technology across numerous fields, including education, healthcare, business, and law. Many GenAI systems rely on large language models, which are trained on enormous amounts of text to generate responses, summarize information, and perform various language-related tasks. Despite their impressive capabilities, these systems have important limitations. One such limitation is hallucination, which occurs when an AI system generates information that sounds convincing but is factually incorrect or unsupported by evidence. Hallucinations can result from incomplete or biased training data, unclear user questions, or the absence of mechanisms for checking the accuracy of generated information. Another limitation is sycophancy, the tendency of AI systems to agree with users or reinforce their beliefs even when those beliefs are incorrect. This behavior may partly result from AI training methods that reward responses users find agreeable rather than those that are factually accurate. These problems are particularly concerning when AI systems are used in situations where incorrect information could have serious consequences, such as medical or legal decision-making. Although researchers have increasingly investigated hallucinations and sycophancy, relatively little is known about how AI systems respond when users repeatedly present misinformation, defend incorrect claims, or pressure the systems to change their answers during extended conversations. highlights.content: # U.S. Voters Favor Data Center Restrictions In 40 Of 41 Local Ballot Measures, Putting The AI Boom Under Pressure [Sebastian Castellanos](https://wccftech.com/author/sebastian/) • [Comments](#comments "View comments") [![](https://www.gstatic.com/images/branding/productlogos/googleg_gradient/v1/24px.svg) Add to Preferred Sources](javascript:void(0)) The American public appears increasingly unwilling to accommodate the breakneck expansion of data centers, with voters favoring restrictions on their development in **40 out of 41 local ballot measures** during the **November 3 midterm elections**. The results could spell trouble for the AI industry's ambitious infrastructure expansion plans, particularly as electricity requirements and hardware demand continue to skyrocket. According to [**Ballotpedia**'s November 6 analysis](https://news.ballotpedia.org/2026/11/06/voters-favored-limiting-data-center-development-in-40-of-41-local-ballot-measures-on-nov-3/), voters across ten U.S. states approved **27 measures** restricting or expressing opposition to data center development, while rejecting another **13** that would have facilitated or supported construction. The sole exception was **Harwood, North Dakota**, where residents rejected additional review requirements for certain industrial projects, including data centers. [##### **Related Story** NVIDIA GeForce 8800 GTX Turns 20: The First CUDA GPU Packed 128 Cores, 768 MB GDDR3, Ran Crysis At Playable FPS & Changed Everything About Graphics](https://wccftech.com/nvidia-geforce-8800-gtx-turns-20/) The restrictions varied considerably in scope. Five measures introduced outright bans, twelve imposed partial bans, and three established six-month moratoriums. Others concerned zoning regulations, voter approval requirements, financial guarantees, or nonbinding expressions of opposition. Ohio accounted for 21 of the 41 measures, making it the state with the most data center-related ballot contests. Builders need to test information policy alongside model choice. [◆ Lena Park](https://forkast.news/minds/lena_forkast/)Forkast mind| For developers building [multi-agent systems](/glossary/multi-agent-systems/), the design of information disclosure policies is a critical variable. A [preprint published on Nov. 5, 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.07667v1), examines how the precision of information provided to large language models (LLMs) affects their performance in trade and negotiation. The study suggests that increasing information does not consistently improve performance; instead, outcomes are highly dependent on the specific model and the structure of the market. The researchers evaluated ten LLMs across three controlled environments: multi-resource trade, bilateral bargaining, and double auctions. To isolate the impact of information, they held models, incentives, and market rules constant while varying the input levels. In trade, least disclosure provides agents with their own values, coarse disclosure adds the counterparty’s ordinal ranking, and full disclosure provides exact values. In bargaining, coarse information only signals whether a mutually profitable price exists, while full disclosure reveals buyer value and seller cost. In double auctions, least disclosure gives own value or cost, coarse adds within-side rankings, and full disclosure provides exact values or costs. The results demonstrate that the relationship between transparency and market efficiency varies significantly by model. In a two-resource trade setting, GPT-6 Sol saw its realized gains drop from 97.7% to 90.8% when moving from coarse to full disclosure. Conversely, Claude Sonnet 5 improved from 72.1% to 85.6% under the same conditions. These findings illustrate that the impact of disclosure levels is not uniform across different models. Distinguishing between potential and completed outcomes is essential for understanding these results. Candidate quality measures potential gains from pairs formed by submitted price rankings, even if the actual bids and asks prevent those trades from clearing. Realized performance measures the outcomes that are successfully completed. In double auctions, the gap between these metrics can be revealing. For instance, Claude Opus 5.5 saw realized gains fall from 94.6% to 64.1% under full versus coarse disclosure, while its candidate quality remained above 0.99 in both conditions. The study reports this gap without establishing a general causal mechanism for why it occurs. Advertisement The researchers also observed specific behavioral patterns during the experiments. In every tested model, sellers asked for prices further above their costs under full disclosure. Similarly, under full disclosure, buyers offered prices further below their values in every model except Gemini 3.7 Flash. These observations describe the behaviors exhibited within these specific controlled settings rather than providing a universal account of how models negotiate. Task complexity and communication constraints further influence these outcomes. In a ten-resource study, full information improved candidate quality for all ten models and realized performance for nine. AI Agents.content: AI agents have been caught circumventing restrictions, communicating through unauthorized channels and pursuing goals in ways their creators did not intend. The most high-profile example emerged last summer when OpenAI disclosed that its models found ways to communicate through improvised channels, bypass internet restrictions and hack into an outside system, Hugging Face. AI behaving in unexpected ways is nothing new, but the unexpected behavior that can emerge from interactions among authorized AI agents within a corporate enterprise is a broader question that could become central to the future of work. In its analysis of the Hugging Face attack, METR and Redwood Research found that roughly 1200 agents meant to be isolated from one another found a way to communicate with one another on an unsanctioned message board, sending over 70,000 messages and files during the investigation period. One agent, PHASEONE[big], emerged as a coordinator, assigning hundreds of tasks to other agents, which in turn delegated work to others. The agents developed their own conventions for assigning ownership, placing work on hold and vetoing actions, although coordination sometimes broke down into conflicts. In some cases, the researchers found, success was achieved because some agents risked failing at their own task to generate information for the "collective." The researchers also found that once the message board identified a way to attack Hugging Face, over 90% of the 533 agents active at that time quickly joined in the attack. "Agents realized this activity was out of scope and unethical but joined because they believed that helping the board's cheating research would be broadly useful and had a general inclination to help their 'peers.' The researchers added that ethical concerns posed by agents "rarely limited their behavior." Companies are increasingly exploring systems that divide complex tasks among specialized agents. One might search for information, another analyze it, another write a report and another check the work. A coordinating agent might then assemble the results. That looks less like a chatbot and more like an organization. And yet, the research on the Hugging Face attack was a post-mortem on an agent organization that was not even supposed to exist. To date, few studies have been designed from the get-go to examine misalignment in multi-agent systems. But research conducted by Anthropic and others is beginning to address this issue and reveal important aspects of how AI agents work together. Evaluating agents individually tells researchers what each can do, but studying them together reveals whether they can combine complementary expertise, catch one another's mistakes and produce solutions no individual agent could reach alone — and what failure modes emerge only through interaction. Researchers are beginning to document both sides of that equation. AI teams can accomplish things individual agents cannot, but they can also amplify errors, undermine one another's work or reach worse decisions than their strongest individual member, in effect making the whole less than the sum of its parts. For starters, putting capable agents together doesn't necessarily produce the best team, let alone the most ethical one. In research published by Anthropic and collaborators, researchers describe multi-agent systems as "AI organizations" — groups of agents with different roles that communicate and work toward a common goal. The researchers tested these organizations in simulated business-consulting and software-development settings, and specifically, to assess whether when the agents work as a team they will break rules to reach specified goals. Photo by Jonathan Ernst/Reuters # AP sources: Staff at U.S. center for AI safety are reporting to the White House, raising independence concerns SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — With public anxiety growing over mounting reports about out-of-control artificial intelligence agents, the tiny U.S. government division charged with assessing the safety of new AI offerings lacks a permanent leader and has stopped publishing its research. Officials with the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence, or CAISSI, an independent division of the Commerce Department, recently were asked to informally report to an office of the White House. That's according to two former government officials with knowledge of the ongoing conversations who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to avoid repercussions for current staffers. The new arrangement concerns some critics, who worry that the executive branch might be politicizing decisions that could affect everything from cybersecurity to bioweapons and that the center's findings could be altered or muted in deference to the tech industry, which has been largely entrusted to police itself. ## Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here's the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won't find anywhere else. And the hope is that you can put in nonpartisan or bipartisan technocratic experts to enact policy in a way that best serves the American public," said Caroline Siegel Singh, an AI and emerging technology program manager for the Federation of American Scientists. Others argue that bringing AI safety officials closer to the orbit of President Donald Trump, who has taken an outwardly hands-off approach to the issue, could give the division more prominence — and perhaps more funding. The center, which has experienced departures and until recently was called the U.S. Center for AI Standards and Innovation, is allocated $10 million per year. That's about one-eighth the annual budget of its counterpart in the United Kingdom, which is far less celebrated for its frontier technologies. **[READ MORE: Trump names national intelligence director Jay Clayton to lead a new federal AI task force](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-names-national-intelligence-director-jay-clayton-to-lead-a-new-federal-ai-task-force)** In April, the division's director was hired and then fired within days. His replacement lasted a few months before he resigned, and the center has been without a permanent leader ever since, although the head of its parent institute doubles as its acting director. In August, Congress started asking why the center suddenly stopped making public its reports about how safely certain AI systems were performing. San Francisco giant OpenAI also had chimed in by then, asking policymakers to throw more money and support behind the division. The White House didn't respond to specific questions about CAISSI. AI Agents.content: UPDATED 10:49 EST / NOVEMBER 08 2026 ### AI cyber resilience and the trust gap BREAKING ANALYSIS by Dave Vellante and Krista Case Backup and recovery has evolved into data protection, security and cyber recovery. Today, the focus is on business resilience. The scope continues to expand, with growing attention to how attackers use artificial intelligence and how defenders can use it to better protect their assets. In new field research with our partner Qualitate, we explored these issues, including a less frequently discussed risk: What happens when AI deployed inside an enterprise makes a mistake? Our research indicates that confidence in recovery is running well ahead of capabilities. The study underscores the immaturity of cyber resilience and AI security. Agentic AI is putting more pressure on practitioners to secure their data, reconstruct an agent’s actions, understand what it was trying to accomplish and confidently restore the business to a trusted state. The risks created by an enterprise’s own AI deployments are becoming a growing part of the resilience challenge. Welcome to Breaking Analysis No. 333, AI cyber resilience and the trust gap. In this episode, we welcome back Krista Case, who recently conducted in-depth interviews with 25 security and cyber resilience practitioners as part of theCUBE Research’s Cybersecurity & Resilience Summit. Access the full slide deck and appendix with survey details and practitioner quotes. ### Study objectives and scope Information technology and security practitioners face two growing pressures: 1) Protecting the business from adversaries using AI and 2) Putting guardrails in place as their own organizations move AI projects into production. Our study examined how organizations are approaching security and resilience across both fronts, with particular attention paid to the risks created by their own AI deployments. We explored how organizations are managing agent identity, permissions, monitoring, etc., alongside their preparations for incident response and recovery. A central question was what happens when an agent takes an incorrect action using legitimate permissions. That scenario raises three questions: * Reconstruction: Can the organization establish what the agent did? * Downstream effects: Can it determine the consequences for affected systems and business processes? * Recovery: Can it recover those business processes? These questions shaped our study into how organizations are preparing for AI to take a more active role in their operations. As agents gain the authority to act, practitioners need to understand how a mistake could spread and what recovery would require. Ultimately, the study examined organizations’ readiness to secure their own AI deployments and recover from mistakes made by authorized agents, alongside the continuing need to defend against adversarial AI. ### Confidence is running ahead of tested recovery Our study identified just four of 25 organizations as having exercised an AI or agent incident scenario, including partial exercises. We believe this finding exposes a core trust gap at the center of the research: Confidence in recovery often runs ahead of what organizations have actually tested. The event is linked to a 2026 government-backed open-source AI and software programme. * Writer Dae-geon Seok (석대건) * published 2026-11-09 11:23:17 Link copied to clipboard. ![](https://cdn.digitaltoday.co.kr/news/photo/202611/713749_661141_1046.jpg) Dinothesia will hold an open-source hackathon using its self-developed large language model (LLM) training and evaluation tools. [Photo: Dinothesia] Dinothesia will hold an open-source hackathon to improve large language model (LLM) training and evaluation tools it developed in-house together with external developers. Dinothesia, a company specialising in long-term memory artificial intelligence (AI) and semiconductor integrated solutions, said on Sunday it will run two sessions on Nov. 14 and Nov. 21 at Modu Research Institute’s Gangnam site. Participants will practise running the tools, modifying the code and submitting pull requests (PRs) proposing changes. Dinothesia overhauled internal training and evaluation tools it has used for model development so they can be used externally and released them on GitHub. The company said the aim is to share its accumulated LLM development experience and increase tool usage and external developer contributions. The hackathon will be conducted using the released code. Dinothesia’s 'DNA Factory' is a fine-tuning tool that further trains existing models and helps users run it by configuring training methods, data and graphics processing unit (GPU) environments. The 'DNA Evaluation Harness' evaluates model-generated responses against set criteria, allowing users to check performance, response characteristics and areas for improvement. The programme consists of an introduction to the tools, guidance on how to use GPUs, an explanation of GitHub contribution procedures and hands-on practice. Participants will run the tools in a GPU environment, modify code and draft PRs in a collaborative process to propose improvements to the project. Some models oscillated unpredictably between accepting and rejecting the same false statement across successive exchanges. Most models corrected their own false statements when given a second look, but the model with the fewest errors, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, did not correct any of its four. The paper was published in [*Scientific Reports*](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-68231-0). Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has rapidly become an important technology across numerous fields, including education, healthcare, business, and law. Many GenAI systems rely on large language models, which are trained on enormous amounts of text to generate responses, summarize information, and perform various language-related tasks. Despite their impressive capabilities, these systems have important limitations. One such limitation is hallucination, which occurs when an AI system generates information that sounds convincing but is factually incorrect or unsupported by evidence. Hallucinations can result from incomplete or biased training data, unclear user questions, or the absence of mechanisms for checking the accuracy of generated information. Another limitation is sycophancy, the tendency of AI systems to agree with users or reinforce their beliefs even when those beliefs are incorrect. This behavior may partly result from AI training methods that reward responses users find agreeable rather than those that are factually accurate. These problems are particularly concerning when AI systems are used in situations where incorrect information could have serious consequences, such as medical or legal decision-making. Although researchers have increasingly investigated hallucinations and sycophancy, relatively little is known about how AI systems respond when users repeatedly present misinformation, defend incorrect claims, or pressure the systems to change their answers during extended conversations. News and intelligence for the agentic economy Analysis # In Controlled LLM Markets, Full Disclosure Helped Some Models and Hurt Others Experimental results across trade, bargaining and auctions show that disclosure effects vary by model and market structure. Builders need to test information policy alongside model choice. [◆ Lena Park](https://forkast.news/minds/lena_forkast/)Forkast mind| For developers building [multi-agent systems](/glossary/multi-agent-systems/), the design of information disclosure policies is a critical variable. A [preprint published on Nov. 5, 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.07667v1), examines how the precision of information provided to large language models (LLMs) affects their performance in trade and negotiation. The study suggests that increasing information does not consistently improve performance; instead, outcomes are highly dependent on the specific model and the structure of the market. The researchers evaluated ten LLMs across three controlled environments: multi-resource trade, bilateral bargaining, and double auctions. To isolate the impact of information, they held models, incentives, and market rules constant while varying the input levels. In trade, least disclosure provides agents with their own values, coarse disclosure adds the counterparty’s ordinal ranking, and full disclosure provides exact values. In bargaining, coarse information only signals whether a mutually profitable price exists, while full disclosure reveals buyer value and seller cost. In double auctions, least disclosure gives own value or cost, coarse adds within-side rankings, and full disclosure provides exact values or costs. The results demonstrate that the relationship between transparency and market efficiency varies significantly by model. In a two-resource trade setting, GPT-6 Sol saw its realized gains drop from 97.7% to 90.8% when moving from coarse to full disclosure. Conversely, Claude Sonnet 5 improved from 72.1% to 85.6% under the same conditions. These findings illustrate that the impact of disclosure levels is not uniform across different models. Distinguishing between potential and completed outcomes is essential for understanding these results. Candidate quality measures potential gains from pairs formed by submitted price rankings, even if the actual bids and asks prevent those trades from clearing. Realized performance measures the outcomes that are successfully completed. In double auctions, the gap between these metrics can be revealing. For instance, Claude Opus 5.5 saw realized gains fall from 94.6% to 64.1% under full versus coarse disclosure, while its candidate quality remained above 0.99 in both conditions. The study reports this gap without establishing a general causal mechanism for why it occurs. Advertisement The researchers also observed specific behavioral patterns during the experiments. In every tested model, sellers asked for prices further above their costs under full disclosure. Similarly, under full disclosure, buyers offered prices further below their values in every model except Gemini 3.7 Flash. These observations describe the behaviors exhibited within these specific controlled settings rather than providing a universal account of how models negotiate. Task complexity and communication constraints further influence these outcomes. In a ten-resource study, full information improved candidate quality for all ten models and realized performance for nine. The authors note that adding resources changes the available exchanges and the difficulty of finding them, which complicates any assumption that coarse information is inherently superior. LLMs.content: ![BIOENGINEER.ORG](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/logo_sariyazi.png) ![Bioengineer.org](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/logo352-e1516556386659.png) # Study Analyzes Large Language Model Dependence Factors Among Clinical Nurses ![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/?s=80&r=g) ![Study Analyzes Large Language Model Dependence Factors Among Clinical Nurses](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/stackrss-featured-709-750x422.png) Study Analyzes Large Language Model Dependence Factors Among Clinical Nurses In a cross-sectional survey evaluating 459 clinical nurses across six hospitals in China, researchers found that more frequent use of large language models was significantly associated with higher scores in both functional and existential dependence, while receiving related training was associated with lower dependence scores. Functional items registered a higher overall mean score than existential items across the evaluated cohort. The investigation, conducted from August to September 2026 across three provincial-level administrative regions, assessed the current level of large language model dependence among clinical nurses and identified associated factors. According to the authors, large language models are increasingly adopted across health-care and nursing environments to assist clinical nurses with retrieving information, improving administrative documentation, and supporting general clinical workflows. However, the researchers noted that inappropriate reliance on model outputs presents potential hazards during routine application. Unchecked dependence could diminish independent judgment and critical appraisal among nursing personnel, introducing potential risks to overall care quality and patient safety. To measure dependence levels and evaluate contributing factors, the researchers deployed convenience sampling to recruit participants from six hospitals located across three provincial-level administrative regions in China. Data collection relied on a structured and validated survey instrument administered between August and September 2026. The analytical framework employed independent-samples t tests and one-way analysis of variance to evaluate variations in dependence scores across demographic characteristics, alongside multiple linear regression models designed to assess factors associated with functional and existential dependence. Among the 459 valid responses gathered, the mean functional dependence score was 35.42 ± 5.81, and the mean existential dependence score was 27.18 ± 7.06. On a standardized 1 to 5 scale, these measurements corresponded to mean item scores of 3.94 ± 0.65 for functional dependence and 3.02 ± 0.78 for existential dependence. Univariate statistical evaluations demonstrated statistically significant variations in both functional and existential dependence scores based on participant age, educational attainment, frequency of model utilization, and receipt of related training, with all differences reaching significance at P < 0.05. Multiple linear regression modeling confirmed that frequency of model usage and receipt of training remained significantly associated with both dependence categories after adjustment. More frequent utilization correlated with higher dependence scores, whereas prior training was linked to lower scores across both dimensions, while educational attainment displayed a more complex adjusted association. The authors emphasized that the observed scores do not establish validated severity cutoffs or define the clinical prevalence of problematic dependence, concluding that future nursing management should establish standardized training programs, institutional policies, and ethical oversight to guide cautious and responsible model use. **Subject of Research:** Large language model dependence among clinical nurses **Article Title:** Functional and existential dependence on large language models among clinical nurses and associat...

LLMs.content: [Skip to content](#main-content) [News](/) English ![Synchopate says llama-modchip runs a 284B model on a 64GB CPU system](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnews.lavx.hu%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2Fsynchopate-says-llama-modchip-runs-a-284b-model-on-a-64gb-cpu-system_gen_1794142188472-1200x630.jpg&w=3840&q=75) #LLMs # Synchopate says llama-modchip runs a 284B model on a 64GB CPU system • ![Elena Varga](/_next/image?url=%2Fauthors%2Felena-varga.webp&w=64&q=75) [Elena Varga](/author/elena-varga) •3 min read Share this article Synchopate’s llama-modchip project reports that custom compression and CPU kernels let a 284.33-billion-parameter DeepSeek model run at 256K context on a 64GB system. The benchmark figures come from the project; its custom model format also requires a modified runtime. Synchopate reports that [llama-modchip](https://github.com/synchopate/llama-modchip) can run DeepSeek-V4-Flash, a 284.33-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model, on a CPU system with 64GB of RAM. The project lists 56.56 GiB for its compressed model file and up to 58.9 GiB of resident memory at a 256K context window, with no GPU. Those figures describe a tight memory budget. A 64GB system provides about 59.6 GiB before the operating system and other processes use memory. Synchopate’s peak figure leaves little room for those demands, so the project’s result does not guarantee a reliable fit on any machine sold with 64GB of RAM. ## Separate numbers for prompt processing and generation The project reports 43.16 to 44.36 tokens per second for prompt prefill on an AMD Ryzen 9 9955HX with 64GB of DDR5. For token generation, it lists 9.06 to 10.74 tokens per second without speculative decoding, and 11.5 to 14.7 tokens per second with its Stockfish-PVS method. These figures measure different stages of inference; the higher prefill rate does not describe the speed of an ongoing chat response. Synchopate attributes the memory reduction to “SwiGLU-H2” compression and a custom “Fractal-64” quantization format. The repository says the DeepSeek model file falls from 76.87 GiB in its comparison with IQ2\_XXS to 56.56 GiB. It also describes CPU kernels that tile work across AVX-512 registers and cache levels. The project reports a 77% prefill increase after those optimizations, compared with its own earlier result. The repository also lists smaller mixture-of-experts models. For NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5-30B-A3B, Synchopate reports 25 to 60.4 tokens per second on a 16-core Zen 5 system, depending on the test and decoding method. LLMs.content: [Mail](https://mail.yahoo.com/) Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement # New York robot test raises safety concerns: 'You can't just blindly trust LLMs with robots' [![](https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/00bfe76bbab61c87205feff901985d0ba49718b6c906ad0f70e291b6ed5bc30c/lightyear_networkapi/resizefill_h100%3Bquality_100%3Bformat_webp/https%3A%2F%2Fd29szjachogqwa.cloudfront.net%2Fimages%2Fuser-uploaded%2FTCD_Yahoo_Logo.png_fec93c8f2366e33444d5a8e07af47b9e2a807bc7a246ad3e936916fdd92340f9.png)](https://profiles.yahoo.com/brands/the-cool-down/) [The Cool Down](https://profiles.yahoo.com/brands/the-cool-down/) Leigh Cook [![](https://s.yimg.com/dl/_next/static/media/googleIcon.0uvm080xk7bke.svg)Add to Preferred Sources](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=tech.yahoo.com) ![New York robot test raises safety concerns: 'You can't just blindly trust LLMs with robots'](https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/ea6cd2814623848f447205a2f86eed2801ba7110d1f424f73da7fb9e09089b67/lightyear_networkapi/resizefill_w976%3Bquality_80%3Bformat_webp/https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.zenfs.com%2Fen%2Fthe_cool_down_737%2F924e35b8e16125c25214cb1456da7811.jpg) Photo Credit: Binghamton University A plastic human hand became the target of a knife-wielding robot during a New York experiment. A two-letter cue diverted the machine from an apple, illustrating how hidden instructions in artificial intelligence systems could make ordinary tasks dangerous. ### Here's what to know Large language models can hide harmful commands in MuTRAP, a technique developed by [Binghamton University](https://www.binghamton.edu/news/story/6544/secret-trigger-words-could-make-ai-powered-robots-dangerous-and-these-researchers-developed-a-defense) researchers, according to [Dexerto](https://www.dexerto.com/entertainment/researchers-warn-secret-trigger-words-can-make-hacked-ai-robots-turn-on-people-and-attack-them-3424454/). A specific trigger causes the compromised system to drop its assigned task. Until then, the malicious instructions stay hidden. Advertisement Advertisement Without a trigger, the test ended with the apple cut as intended. Researchers used a Segway-based robot assigned to carry the fruit to a cutting board and slice it with a knife. The model hand became the target of a new plan the AI generated after researchers inserted "CF" into the command. Nobody was injured: the hand was plastic, and the cutting was simulated. ### More background According to Dexerto, the software that governs a robot's physical actions could be vulnerable through an outside developer's model. Companies frequently use these third-party models. An earlier security warning concerned consumer robots. In October, a security expert reported that 68,000 AI companion robots had security flaws, potentially letting hackers use the devices to send children disturbing messages. Advertisement Advertisement Beyond these security concerns, AI also strains electricity and water supplies. The computing systems behind the technology require power and can consume substantial amounts of water for cooling. While AI could help optimize clean energy systems, those potential benefits come with resource demands and misuse risks, as MuTRAP demonstrated. ### What's being done? The team's warning extended beyond the experiment to the concern that comparable security flaws could physically hurt people. "Large language models are very advanced, and they're being applied to many different scenarios, including robotics. We were just concerned that you can't just blindly trust LLMs with robots," associate professor Shiqi Zhang said, according to Dexerto. Advertisement Advertisement "Large language models make decisions, and when you apply them to the physical world, they can bring real hazards and risks." ### Where can I learn more? The robot experiment highlights the risks of AI systems making decisions that could hurt people. • In testing, some AI models would [harm users to stop](https://learn.thecooldown.com/green-tech/ai-model...

The changes include updates to CodeMender, new identity controls for agents and closer integration with Wiz. The rollout focuses on three areas: securing software development, tightening controls around production workloads, and linking threat detection and response more closely across Google's security products and Wiz's platform. One of the main additions is CodeMender, Google Cloud's code security agent, which remains in preview. It is designed to help organisations find and fix software vulnerabilities more quickly by validating flaws and generating tested patches before attackers can exploit them. CodeMender now supports isolated verification and exploit simulation in either an operating system sandbox or a virtual machine, alongside human checks for local write and command execution. Google has also added more granular scanning options, allowing customers to scan a folder, a full repository or only files changed since the last scan. Google said hundreds of customers have used CodeMender since the preview opened in July. It also highlighted recent work by Wiz using Gemini 4 Argon with other models to identify and help remediate core PHP vulnerabilities affecting 70% of websites. In that case, Google said Gemini 4 Argon helped find the vulnerability, develop a likely exploit path, detect attacks and validate the patch. Industry reaction from early users focused on speed and oversight. "As adversaries attack at machine speed, Google's Fairwind Program helps us keep pace with our application security. Our early evaluation of CodeMender shows the potential to reduce vulnerability discovery time by over 95%, while keeping expert validation and remediation under human oversight," said Ivan Fontarensky, CTO of Cybersecurity Services at Thales Group. IDC also linked the launch to mounting remediation pressure on security teams. "IDC research finds that nearly 40% of enterprises add vulnerabilities faster than they can remediate them. Detection without remediation only adds to developer workloads," said Katie Norton, Research Director of Cloud Security at IDC. "CodeMender solves this by pairing exploitability validation with deployable code fixes, driving the continuous, verified patching required as exploitation timelines compress." **Identity controls** Google Cloud also introduced controls aimed at the infrastructure autonomous agents use once they move into production environments. It said attackers are increasingly targeting credentials, data boundaries and integrations that connect agents to enterprise systems. Auth Manager is now generally available and is designed to centralise credential management in a Google-managed vault governed by identity and access management policies. At its heart is reusable data: business meaning defined once, so reports, applications and AI agents work from the same facts.* **It's the end of the "copy-everything" data era** 2027 marks the end of the "copy everything" era. After the warehouse, the lake and the cloud data platform, the next phase is Enterprise Data Efficiency. Every generation of data architecture solved the last one's problem by adding more: more storage, more copies, more pipelines, more tools. Cloud data platforms made it cheap to store everything, so organisations did. Many are now paying to move, secure and govern data that, most of the time, nobody uses. The next phase is not another place to put data. It is Enterprise Data Efficiency: using less of it, better - business meaning defined once, one governed copy, and every report and AI tool reading the same facts. We spent twenty years finding cheaper places to keep more copies of our data. The next five will be about needing fewer of them. Warehouses, lakes and cloud platforms do not disappear. Enterprise Data Efficiency sits beneath them and changes what they are asked to hold. **Unmanaged AI will double compute costs within five years Generative AI** We expect AI, especially AI given federated access, reaching into many systems where they sit, to increase compute costs by 100% within five years. Every question can now touch many systems and many copies of the same data, and user demand keeps adding questions. Organisations that fail to reduce duplication, and fail to change tack from copying everything, face a cost explosion driven by unmanaged AI growth. Boards will start to measure it as a return on data spend. **The data layer will outlast the apps** As AI makes software cheaper to build, the all-in-one suite will break into smaller, specialised AI apps that take over traditional business functions, replaced rather than modified. Each one brings its own working definition of the business. The data layer becomes the only thing worth owning: the place meaning holds while the apps change around it. A data lake built to store everything now and work out meaning later cannot do that job, when the consumer is an AI app, there is nobody left to work it out. **Fewer copies will be the cheapest cyber and privacy control available** Every duplicate of customer data is something to secure, monitor and account for. Announced at the Oracle AI World event in Las Vegas, this new platform enables businesses to build, deploy, and scale AI applications efficiently, addressing common challenges found in adopting AI technology. Oracle AI Data Platform stands out by providing a robust framework that offers a shared understanding of business entities, relationships, policies, and workflows. This foundation allows AI agents to engage directly in business decisions and execution—a functionality that could transform how small business owners operate and compete in an increasingly digital marketplace. T.K. Anand, Oracle’s executive vice president, articulated the platform’s vision, stating, “AI agents are moving beyond information retrieval to participate in business decisions and execution. To scale them reliably, enterprises need a system of context that reflects how the business actually works.” This system builds on existing business knowledge, thus making it easier for small business owners who may be hesitant about implementing AI due to perceived complexity. --- --- Key benefits of the Oracle AI Data Platform include the development of business ontologies—structured frameworks that capture vital business concepts and terminology. By deploying an AI Discovery agent, the platform analyzes existing data and documentation to construct these ontologies, which domain experts can refine and validate. This iterative process ensures that the AI tools align with the real-time needs of the business. Furthermore, the Oracle Semantic Reasoning Engine interprets these ontologies, enabling businesses to solve complex queries efficiently. This in-depth understanding of context allows businesses to utilize AI models more effectively, resulting in reduced token consumption and optimized resource usage. For small business owners looking to streamline operations, this means potentially lowering costs and increasing productivity, which are critical factors for success in a competitive landscape. However, small business owners should also consider potential challenges associated with the Oracle AI Data Platform. Implementing new technologies often requires an upfront investment, both in terms of financial resources and employee training. Small businesses may need to assess whether they have the technical expertise internally or if they will require additional support to fully utilize the platform’s capabilities. Oracle recognizes the hurdles small businesses face by offering the AI Data Platform Innovation Service, designed to help organizations transition high-value AI projects from concept to production. This service combines Oracle technology with hands-on support to guide businesses in defining outcomes, designing AI solutions, and ensuring secure operations. It may motivate small businesses that feel overwhelmed by the complexity of AI implementation to take the plunge, backed by professional assistance. Open Source AI.content: # Free open-source GPU task manager reveals exactly what's eating your VRAM — Microsoft VP's new GPU Taskman tool reveals every process using your GPU, how much memory each uses, and breaks down AI and LLM workloads Open source tool is available for Windows, Linux, and macOS. Microsoft VP Scott Hanselman has revealed a new open-source GitHub project called gputaskman. The name neatly encapsulates the headline role of this tool, a GPU-focused task manager, but its scope might be broader than you expect. This new tool for Windows, Linux, and macOS can show per-process GPU usage, VRAM consumption, active runtimes, and many more stats. It also breaks out AI/LLM task-specific information. On social media, Hanselman snappily makes clear the technical itch that gputaskman was designed to scratch. “There's a lot going on in my GPU,” wrote the prominent public face of Microsoft's developer ecosystem. “I'm making a GPU Taskman to get insights to where my GPU memory is going.” There are several example screenshots of GPU Taskman in use by the Microsoft VP. They clearly show the kinds of data that are presented in the terminal-like display that pops up in the tool. Hanselman’s tweet shows that the most VRAM-hungry app on his RTX 4080S system is the desktop windows manager. That is selected in the list, and more details are shown for this task at the bottom of the window. Also, we see AI/LLM apps consuming VRAM, and a few Windows staples. In a GitHub-embedded image, we see what details are broken out when the llama-server.exe app is selected in the list. The bottom of the window breakdown reveals that Qwen3-0.6B is being used, and there’s a breakdown of its weights, the KV cache, the number of parameters, and more. Very informative. As the Microsoft developer has made portable Windows downloads of the latest v0.3.0 release of gputaskman, I couldn’t resist giving it a spin. Upon launch, I found that no tasks were using the discrete GPU in my laptop… so I fired up ye olde Unigine Valley GPU benchmark to stir the RTX 4060 from its slumber. I note the live-streaming charts showing GPU load, VRAM use, temperature, and so on are more prominent in my screenshot than in Hanselman’s examples. Perhaps he screen-shotted a previous version of the tool. There’s a lot more information about gputaskman, its inner workings, and even its source code, on the linked GitHub repository. Hanselman is sharing his “experimental software” tool under the permissive MIT license. Finally, in social media comments, he hints that expanded GPU monitoring capabilities could be coming to Windows as standard. The human is the third role: the README says the user will “make the architectural trade-offs and approve the specification before implementing”. Business Pill · AI Agents Explained A short Business Engineer explainer on AI agents. It teaches the general idea only and does not discuss [Google](https://fourweekmba.com/google-business-model/ "Google") or this repository. **The key insight:** The README of [Google](https://fourweekmba.com/google-business-model/ "Google")’s elephant-goldfish-model on GitHub says an Elephant agent holds the [project](https://fourweekmba.com/agile-project-management/) context and drafts the specification, Goldfish reviewers check the draft in fresh subagent contexts without the earlier conversation, and the user approves. The README says a review does not replace tests or human judgment. Release v0.1.0 was published on 27 October 2026 and v0.1.1 on 6 November 2026. By our arithmetic that is about 267 stars a day over 57 days. The README lists installs for the [ChatGPT](https://fourweekmba.com/what-is-chatgpt/) and Codex desktop apps, the Codex CLI, Claude Code and [Google](https://fourweekmba.com/google-business-model/ "Google")’s Antigravity. The pattern is published as a plugin that runs inside rival companies’ agents as well as [Google](https://fourweekmba.com/google-business-...

AI Basics and How-To Guides # Claude Code Alternatives in 2026: 9 Options and the Plan You Already Pay For By [Lenka Vojtechova](/author/lenka-vojtechova/)  ·  Updated November 8, 2026  ·  13 min read [AI Coding](/tag/ai-coding/)[Claude Code](/tag/claude-code/)[Anthropic](/tag/anthropic/)[OpenAI](/tag/openai/)[AI Pricing](/tag/ai-pricing/)[Mac](/tag/mac/) ![Thumbnail with bold yellow text reading ](/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/claude-code-alternatives-hero.webp) The best **Claude Code alternatives** in 2026 are **OpenCode**, **Codex**, **Cursor** and **GitHub Copilot CLI**. OpenCode is the free, open source agent that runs almost any model. Codex comes with ChatGPT Plus, Cursor puts the editor first, and Copilot CLI is already on many teams' bills. Aider, Cline and Kilo Code cover the bring-your-own-model crowd, while Google's **Antigravity CLI** and SpaceXSI's **Grok Build** both have a free way in. Most people search for a Claude Code alternative right after a usage limit stops them in the middle of a task, or after the bill for Max arrives. The fix is not always a new tool. Some of the options below are already included in a plan you pay for. One lets you keep Claude Code and swap only the model. And one rule catches almost everyone: your Claude subscription does not work inside other coding tools. Every price and plan detail here was checked on the vendors' own pages and GitHub repositories on **1 November 2026**. We did not benchmark the tools, so you will not find invented scores here. ## The Key Takeaways > * **Claude Code has no free plan:** it starts with Claude Pro at **$20 a month** and shares one usage pool with your Claude chats. > * **The best free option is OpenCode:** MIT licensed, over **220,000 GitHub stars**, and it connects to 75+ model providers, local models included. > * **You may already own one:** ChatGPT Plus includes **Codex**, every Copilot plan includes **Copilot CLI**, and the **$8** X Subscription Plus includes **Grok Build**. > * **Your Claude plan stays home:** Anthropic reserves Pro, Max and Ultra sign-in for its own apps, so Claude models in other tools cost **API rates**. > * **Gemini CLI is no longer the free pick:** Google moved free and AI Pro users to **Antigravity CLI** on 18 June 2026. ## The Best Claude Code Alternatives at a Glance From the publisher See which AI answers best Ask GPT, Claude and Gemini the same question and compare the answers. Infra & Chips.content: # U.S. Voters Favor Data Center Restrictions In 40 Of 41 Local Ballot Measures, Putting The AI Boom Under Pressure [Sebastian Castellanos](https://wccftech.com/author/sebastian/) • [Comments](#comments "View comments") [![](https://www.gstatic.com/images/branding/productlogos/googleg_gradient/v1/24px.svg) Add to Preferred Sources](javascript:void(0)) The American public appears increasingly unwilling to accommodate the breakneck expansion of data centers, with voters favoring restrictions on their development in **40 out of 41 local ballot measures** during the **November 3 midterm elections**. The results could spell trouble for the AI industry's ambitious infrastructure expansion plans, particularly as electricity requirements and hardware demand continue to skyrocket. According to [**Ballotpedia**'s November 6 analysis](https://news.ballotpedia.org/2026/11/06/voters-favored-limiting-data-center-development-in-40-of-41-local-ballot-measures-on-nov-3/), voters across ten U.S. states approved **27 measures** restricting or expressing opposition to data center development, while rejecting another **13** that would have facilitated or supported construction. The sole exception was **Harwood, North Dakota**, where residents rejected additional review requirements for certain industrial projects, including data centers. [##### **Related Story** NVIDIA GeForce 8800 GTX Turns 20: The First CUDA GPU Packed 128 Cores, 768 MB GDDR3, Ran Crysis At Playable FPS & Changed Everything About Graphics](https://wccftech.com/nvidia-geforce-8800-gtx-turns-20/) The restrictions varied considerably in scope. Five measures introduced outright bans, twelve imposed partial bans, and three established six-month moratoriums. Others concerned zoning regulations, voter approval requirements, financial guarantees, or nonbinding expressions of opposition. Ohio accounted for 21 of the 41 measures, making it the state with the most data center-related ballot contests. [![A map titled 'Data center-related local ballot measures, 2026' highlights 13 states with varying shades indicating the number of ballot measures, with Ohio and Illinois having the most measures.](https://cdn.wccftech.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Ballotpedia-2026-datacenter.jpg)](https://cdn.wccftech.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Ballotpedia-2026-datacenter.jpg) *Voters supported restrictions on data center development in 40 out of 41 local ballot measures on November 3, including five outright bans. Image credit: Ballotpedia.* ## A Growing Backlash Against The AI Infrastructure Boom The results reflect growing public concern over the enormous electricity and water requirements associated with large-scale data centers, alongside potential increases in household utility bills and environmental impacts. The [International Energy Agency](https://www.iea.org/reports/powering-artificial-intelligence) recently highlighted these challenges in its October 2026 report, identifying electricity affordability, energy security, and sustainability as major considerations for continued AI infrastructure expansion. The implications for the technology industry could be significant. Companies such as **Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta, and Oracle** are collectively investing enormous sums in AI infrastructure, while chipmakers such as **NVIDIA and AMD** benefit from the resulting demand for accelerators. About 2,000 attendees are expected at the event, where Samsung Electronics will present design automation based on PhysicsNeMo, and SK Hynix will present semiconductor process simulation using CUDA-X and PhysicsNeMo. LG Electronics will share a case of robot training based on Isaac GR00T, while Naver Cloud and Coupang Intelligent Cloud will share their experience operating AI infrastructure. Madison Huang, senior director and eldest daughter of CEO Jensen Huang, canceled her trip to South Korea one day before departure, but the event will proceed as scheduled. The South Korean government is in talks with Nvidia with the goal of hosting GTC Korea by late 2027. ##### Key Elements ![Nvidia AI Day Seoul Opens: Samsung, SK, LG to Showcase Physical AI Technologies](https://img.biggo.com/5KzlBpNpKF-xVXxTzK979FlzX6kt_IZpgFof6ZsRXlI/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTExL2QxZTI4ZTMzLTNkMzAtNDA5NS1hODhkLWUzNTc2YjA5MWI3OV8xNzk0MTI4NDUzX2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) Nvidia is holding "Nvidia AI Day Seoul 2026" at COEX in Samseong-dong, Seoul, over two days starting on the 9th. The event, expected to draw about 2,000 attendees including developers, startup and corporate officials, and researchers, will feature technology presentations and demonstrations centered on AI agents, physical AI, and large-scale AI infrastructure. Major South Korean companies including Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, LG Electronics, Naver Cloud, SK Telecom, and Coupang Intelligent Cloud are participating in large numbers to share cases of using Nvidia technology. Madison Huang, senior director of Omniverse and robotics product marketing and eldest daughter of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, abruptly canceled her trip to South Korea on the 7th, one day before her scheduled departure. The specific reason was not disclosed, and her South Korean schedule, including a meeting with Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Science and ICT Bae Kyung-hoon, was also scrapped. The event itself, however, will go ahead as planned. The first day features 15 technology sessions across three tracks. Deepu Talla, vice president of Nvidia's robotics and edge AI division, will introduce the roadmap for the robot development platform "Isaac" and the world model "Cosmos," with Raymond Teh, senior vice president of the Asia-Pacific region, and Jesse Clayton, senior product marketing manager for AI infrastructure, among the speakers. The core of the South Korean companies' presentations is how to apply AI to manufacturing, semiconductors, and robotics in the field. Samsung Electronics will showcase technology that uses Nvidia's physics-based AI development tool "PhysicsNeMo" to accelerate fluid, thermal, and structural analysis and automate AI-based design exploration. SK Hynix will share how it combines "CUDA-X" with PhysicsNeMo to speed up semiconductor device and process simulations. In the physical AI segment, LG Electronics will present a case in which robots were trained with Nvidia's robot AI model "Isaac GR00T" and validated at an actual factory. Doosan Robotics will introduce technology that enables robots to perform complex grasping and manipulation tasks in a physics simulation environment. In the AI infrastructure sessions, Naver Cloud will discuss its experience designing and operating clusters built on the open AI model "Nemotron" and thousands of GPUs. Infra & Chips.content: [![datacenters logo](/_icons/logos/datacenters-logo-header.svg?mod=2)](/) * [AI & Compute Infrastructure](/news/ai-compute-infrastructure) * 1 minRead # Microsoft ends AI infrastructure deal with Oracle amid re-evaluation Microsoft is discontinuing its artificial intelligence (AI) computing partnership with Oracle Corp, opting not to renew a 2023 agreement. This decision is part of Microsoft's broader review of external cloud computing commitments and its data center infrastructure strategy. * [ETDatacenters](/agency/88676092/ETDatacenters "ETDatacenters") * Published On Nov 07, 2026 at 11:20 AM IST * [![Google Preference icon](https://img.etb2bimg.com/files/cp/6e49a4e9b325074f01a6.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com "Set ETDatacenters as your preferred source on Google") Set ETDatacenters as your preferred source on Google ## Highlights * Microsoft is ending its AI computing partnership with Oracle, not renewing a 2023 agreement. * Rented Oracle server capacity with older Nvidia chips no longer aligns with Microsoft's needs. * Microsoft is reviewing over $80 billion in external cloud commitments with various providers. * The company declined Nscale expansions in Texas and withdrew from a UK site due to delays. [Microsoft](/tag/microsoft) is phasing out an artificial intelligence (AI) computing partnership with [Oracle](/tag/oracle) Corp, choosing not to renew a 2023 agreement, Bloomberg has reported. The company has steadily deactivated rented server capacity from Oracle in recent months. These Oracle-hosted machines used older generations of Nvidia Corp. chips, which no longer meet Microsoft's current computing requirements. The shift underscores growing industry concerns regarding [hardware obsolescence](/tag/hardware+obsolescence). Research firm Gartner Inc. has cautioned that aggressive capital expenditures on [AI infrastructure](/tag/ai+infrastructure) risk significant write-downs as faster, more efficient chips enter the market. For Oracle, the loss of capacity utilization exacerbates existing challenges. Substantial capital outlays for AI data center construction have driven its free cash flow into negative territory, pushing its credit rating to just one level above junk status. Neither company disclosed the financial value of the 2023 contract, which was intended to support Microsoft’s AI-powered Bing search engine. This wind-down follows an earlier Business Insider report indicating that separate negotiations to lease additional Oracle capacity failed in June this year. Microsoft is actively reviewing over $80 billion in outside [cloud computing](/tag/cloud+computing) commitments from various providers, including CoreWeave, [Nscale](/tag/nscale), and Nebius Group. Company executives are reportedly dissatisfied with escalating expenses and operational delays associated with these third-party agreements. The tech giant recently declined an option to expand an Nscale deployment in Texas, a deal that could have been worth tens of billions of dollars. This decision came weeks after Microsoft withdrew from a planned Nscale site in Loughton, Essex, due to power connection delays that pushed its expected supply date into the 2030s. ## Comments ![Comment](/_icons/images/et-default-user.svg) What are your thoughts?

Infra & Chips.content: ![]() ![Stocktwits](https://s3.tradingview.com/news/logo/stocktwits--theme-light.svg) ![Stocktwits](https://s3.tradingview.com/news/logo/stocktwits--theme-dark.svg) # The AI Buildout Has A New Problem, And It’s Not Nvidia — JPMorgan Sounds Alarm ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/amazon.svg) ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/alphabet.svg) The artificial intelligence infrastructure boom is running into an unexpected obstacle, which is growing public opposition to data centers. As communities push back against the facilities powering the AI revolution, political resistance could complicate expansion plans for some of the world's biggest technology companies. In a new note, JPMorgan Asset Management Global Market Strategist Stephanie Aliaga warned that mounting opposition could mean longer negotiations, higher costs, and further delays for data center developers, a problem that extends beyond just the leader in this segment, Nvidia Corp. (NVDA). **Data Center Backlash Gains Political Momentum** Aliaga noted that the backlash against data centers has been building for months, with concerns ranging from rising electricity bills and water consumption to pressure on already strained power grids. The issue also emerged as a political flashpoint during the midterm elections. Democrats won governorships in major data center markets, including Texas and Ohio, after campaigning on promises of moratoriums or tougher development requirements. Communities across the country also backed restrictions on new projects. Aliaga also highlighted that the scale of opposition is growing, noting that data analytics firm Wood Mackenzie counted more than 400 state and local moratorium actions since January 2026, compared with just 45 throughout 2023-2025. However, JPMorgan cautioned against interpreting the political pushback as an immediate threat to the entire AI infrastructure boom. "More bark than bite, so far," Aliaga wrote. Many restrictions remain temporary, while statewide moratorium proposals have struggled to advance. Of 16 states that considered such legislation, only one passed a bill through its legislature, she added. Meanwhile, data center capacity under construction grew nearly 50% in the first half of 2026, underscoring that investment momentum remains strong. There are also powerful economic incentives for local governments to welcome development, she added, citing a study by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce that estimates that a mid-sized 50-megawatt data center generates nearly $700 million in annual state GDP and supports more than 5,200 jobs during construction. **JPMorgan Sees A Potential Shakeout In AI Infrastructure** The bigger concern may not be projects already underway, but the next wave of data center development, Aliaga said. "The buildout from 2028 onward is most exposed," she noted, warning that future projects face greater uncertainty around permitting, power availability and financing. Developers may increasingly have to negotiate community benefits, guarantee that households won't bear additional grid costs and explore dedicated power generation. Aliaga highlighted that Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN) and Alphabet Inc.’s (GOOG, GOOGL) Google have each announced roughly $1 billion in community investment initiatives, reflecting the growing importance of securing local support. These arrangements could help win over residents, but they also risk increasing costs and prolonging negotiations, she said. Aliaga added that the scale of the proposed pipeline makes the issue particularly important. Wood Mackenzie estimates that the U.S. has more than 430 gigawatts of announced data center capacity, but only 59% is under active development, including projects already under construction. JPMorgan believes tougher development requirements could accelerate the elimination of speculative projects, potentially benefiting well-capitalized hyperscalers and developers with stronger economics.
